entries.title: Lamb and the shank
entries.summary: Lamb is the meat of a sheep under a year old, and its cuts divide by the work the muscle did. The shank, the lower leg, is the slow-cooked cut: it melts over hours into a tender braise and a glossy jus.
entries.guest: Our lamb shank is slow-cooked until it is tender and wrapped in puff pastry, with a jus scented with star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon: warm, not hot.

paras: Lamb is the meat of a young sheep, and the word carries an age. In the United States lamb is a sheep under a year old, most going to market at six to eight months; past a year it is classed as yearling mutton, and older still as mutton, darker and stronger. Hogget, say HOG-it, is the British and New Zealand word for the year-old animal. The taste that makes a guest hesitate lives in the fat: sweet, grassy, a little gamey, stronger with age and a diet of grass. American lamb is larger and milder, often finished on grain; New Zealand and Australian lamb is grass-fed, smaller and more pronounced.

Spring lamb once meant a lamb born in late winter and sold young at Easter. Lambing now runs all year, so the phrase on a label says only that the animal was slaughtered between March and October; the season no longer rules the market.

The cuts sort by the work the muscle did. The rack and the loin did little and are tender, so they take fast heat and are served pink. The leg is lean and large, a roasting cut carved thin. The shoulder and the shank worked hard, and their sinew needs hours of moist heat; a shoulder chop is a bargain for the braise. Buy lamb that is pale pink to light red with firm white fat; dark meat and yellowed fat mean an older animal.

The shank is the lower leg: a bundle of muscle wrapped in sinew around a bone. That sinew is collagen, a protein that stays tough under fast heat and melts into gelatine only when held wet and warm for hours. The change begins above about 70°C (158°F) and runs best in a braise of wine and aromatics held at 85 to 90°C (185 to 194°F), below a boil, for three hours or so; the gelatine then thickens the liquid and coats the meat, so a braised shank feels rich without cream or flour. The meat is done when a fork pulls it from the bone and it still holds together.

The jus, say ZHOO, French for juice, is the meat's own juices made into a sauce: the braise's liquid, or a stock of lamb bones and trimmings, strained, skimmed of fat and reduced until it coats a spoon and shines. The gelatine gives it body, so no roux goes near it.

Ours is scented with star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon, the three the sheet names. The usual way is to steep the spice whole in the reducing liquid, a star or two, a strip of peel, a piece of cinnamon, lifted out before it takes over; which stock, any wine, how far it is reduced and any butter finish are not printed, so learn the build at lineup. Warm and aromatic, never hot: there is no chilli in it.

Tough meat: the braise was too short or too hot; at a boil the meat seizes and dries while its sinew stays firm, so lower the heat and give it time. Meat in threads: cooked too long; stop when the fork turns it. A bitter, medicinal jus: too much spice, or spice left in too long; use it whole, taste often and lift it out.

At Brennan's the shank is the fall Lamb Shank en Croûte, say ahn KROOT, in a crust: a lamb shank daube, say DOHB, wrapped in puff pastry and baked until the pastry is crisp, with the spiced lamb jus of star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon. The braise does the tenderising before the wrapping; the oven's job is the crust. The pack does not print the braising liquid, the portion or whether the bone travels inside the pastry, so learn the build at lineup, and send a question about wine in the braise or butter in the pastry to the kitchen.

Describe lamb as sweet and a little grassy, richer than beef, and the shank as the gentlest way to meet it: slow cooking and trimmed fat soften the taste that worries a guest. A guest who likes beef but is unsure of lamb can be steered to the shank; a guest who wants lamb pink wants a chop or a rack. Say: tender lamb shank, slow-cooked, in a crisp pastry crust, with a jus of star anise, orange and cinnamon, warm rather than hot.

ratios.label: Time in the braise
ratios.value: About three hours below a boil, until a fork pulls the meat from the bone

ratios.label: Reduction of the jus
ratios.value: By half or more, until it coats a spoon and shines

ratios.label: Scenting a jus, the usual way, for about 1 litre (about 1 quart)
ratios.value: One or two stars of anise, a strip of orange peel and a small piece of cinnamon, whole, lifted out when the scent is right

temps.label: Collagen begins to melt into gelatine above about
A braise is held from about

faults.cause: The braise was too short, or ran at a boil, which seizes the meat while the sinew stays firm.
faults.fix: Lower the heat to a bare simmer and give it more time; test with a fork, not a clock.

faults.cause: Cooked too long after the sinew had melted.
faults.fix: Stop when a fork turns the meat and it still holds together; check from the second hour.

faults.cause: The braising liquid was skimmed too little before reducing.
faults.fix: Chill it so the fat sets, lift the fat off, then reduce.

faults.cause: Too much star anise or cinnamon, or whole spice left in too long.
faults.fix: Use the spice whole, taste every few minutes and lift it out; loosen an overspiced jus with plain stock.

brennans.how: The shank is braised as a daube until it is tender, then wrapped in puff pastry; the jus is scented with star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon, warm rather than hot. The braising liquid, the portion and whether the bone travels inside the pastry are not printed: learn them at lineup.

sources.evidence: Lamb is meat from sheep less than 1 year old. Most are brought to market at about 6 to 8 months old. If the phrase Spring Lamb is on a meat label, it means the lamb was slaughtered between March and October.

cards.front: What separates lamb, hogget and mutton?
cards.back: Age. In the United States lamb is under a year old, most at six to eight months; hogget is the British and New Zealand word for the year-old animal; mutton is older, darker, firmer and stronger.

cards.front: Why is American lamb larger and milder than New Zealand's?
cards.back: American lambs go to market heavier and are often finished on grain, which gives bigger cuts and a milder taste; New Zealand and Australian lamb is grass-fed, smaller and more pronounced.

cards.front: What does spring lamb mean today?
cards.back: Once a lamb born in late winter and sold young at Easter. With lambing all year, the label only says the animal was slaughtered between March and October; the season no longer rules the market.

cards.front: Which lamb cuts take fast heat, and which the slow braise?
cards.back: Rack and loin for fast heat and the leg for roasting, since those muscles did little work; shoulder and shank, the working muscles full of sinew, for the slow braise.

cards.front: Why does a shank need hours when a chop needs minutes?
cards.back: It is the lower leg, wrapped in sinew: collagen that stays tough under fast heat and melts into gelatine only when held wet and warm, above about 70°C (158°F), for hours.

cards.front: At what temperature is a shank braise held, and for how long?
cards.back: Below a boil, about 85 to 90°C (185 to 194°F), for three hours or so; at a boil the meat seizes and dries while the sinew stays firm.

cards.front: What is a jus, and how is ours scented?
cards.back: The meat's own juices, the braise's liquid or a lamb stock, strained, skimmed and reduced until they shine, with body from gelatine and never from roux; ours names star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon, warm rather than hot, and the build is a lineup question.

cards.front: How do you know a braised shank is done?
cards.back: A fork pulls the meat from the bone and it still holds together; resistance means more time, and meat in threads means it went too long.

cards.front: How do you describe lamb to a guest who hesitates?
cards.back: Sweet and a little grassy, richer than beef. The taste lives in the fat, so slow cooking and trimmed fat make the shank the gentlest way to meet it.

cards.front: One guest wants lamb pink; another is unsure of lamb at all. Where does each go?
cards.back: Pink wants a chop or a rack, cooked fast and rested; the unsure guest is best served the slow-cooked shank, mild under its pastry and the warm spice of the jus.

cards.front: What is the Lamb Shank en Croûte?
cards.back: A lamb shank daube wrapped in puff pastry and baked crisp, with a jus of star anise, orange and cinnamon. The braising liquid, the portion and whether the bone is inside are not printed: learn them at lineup.

questions.q: In the United States, what makes a sheep's meat lamb rather than mutton?
questions.answer: The animal was under a year old
distractors: The animal was fed only on grass
The meat came from the shank
The animal was born in spring
questions.why: Lamb is the meat of a sheep under a year old, most at six to eight months; past a year it is yearling mutton, then mutton. Diet and cut change the taste, not the name.

questions.q: Which lamb cut belongs in a slow braise rather than on a hot grill?
questions.answer: The shank
questions.why: The shank is a working muscle full of sinew that needs hours of moist heat; rack and loin did little work and take fast heat, and the leg roasts.

questions.q: What happens to the sinew in a shank during a long braise?
questions.answer: Collagen melts into gelatine
questions.why: Collagen stays tough under fast heat but, held wet and warm above about 70°C (158°F) for hours, melts into gelatine, which makes the meat tender and gives the liquid body.

questions.q: A shank braise is bubbling hard on the stove. What should the cook do?
questions.answer: Lower it to below a boil
distractors: Keep it boiling to save time
Pour in cold stock and chill it to stop the cooking
questions.why: A braise is held at about 85 to 90°C (185 to 194°F); at a boil the meat seizes and dries while the sinew stays firm, and only time at low heat melts it.

questions.q: What gives a lamb jus its body?
questions.answer: Gelatine from the braise
questions.why: A jus is the meat's own juices, the braise's liquid or a lamb stock, strained, skimmed and reduced; the gelatine the sinew gave up thickens it, so no roux or cream goes near it.

questions.q: What does the phrase spring lamb on a label mean today?
questions.answer: Slaughtered between March and October
questions.why: Lambing now runs through the year, so the label marks only the slaughter window; the old sense of a late-winter lamb sold young at Easter no longer rules the market.

questions.q: A guest says lamb is too strong for them. How do you describe it?
questions.answer: Sweet, a little grassy, richer than beef
questions.why: Lamb's taste lives in its fat and is sweet and grassy rather than harsh; slow cooking and trimmed fat make the shank the gentlest way to meet it.

questions.q: Which of these does the Brennan's pack print about the Lamb Shank en Croûte?
questions.answer: A jus of star anise, orange and cinnamon
distractors: Whether the bone is inside the pastry
questions.why: The pack names the puff pastry and the spiced jus of star anise, orange and a touch of cinnamon; the braising liquid, the portion and the bone are not printed, so they are lineup questions.

entries.title: Swordfish
entries.summary: A large ocean fish sold as thick steaks or fillets: firm, dense and mildly sweet, cooked more like meat than like a flaky fillet. It dries fast once the centre turns opaque, so it is seared hard, pulled early and rested.
entries.guest: Swordfish is a firm, meaty fish with a mildly sweet taste; ours is cooked to order and finished with brown butter, lemon and fried capers over soft, slow-cooked leeks.

paras: Swordfish is a large, fast fish of warm and temperate seas, named for the flat bill it uses to slash at its prey. It comes to the kitchen as thick steaks cut across the loin, or as thick fillets from the loin, as our sheet prints it, and the flesh is unlike most fish: firm, dense, pale cream to pinkish, mildly sweet and clean, closer to a veal cutlet than to a flake of cod. Cooks treat it as meat, and so do guests who say they do not like fish.

A steak is cut thick, about 3 cm (1 1/4 inches) and never under 2.5 cm (1 inch), because a thin steak is dry before it has a crust. Along the middle runs the bloodline, a band of dark red muscle that tastes strong and metallic: trim it out. The skin is thick and comes off before the pan. Fresh swordfish smells of the sea, with a glossy cut face and no browning at the edges; a yellow tinge or a sour note sends it back.

Pat the steak dry, salt it and oil it lightly. Lay it in a smoking-hot pan or on a hot grill and leave it alone until a crust forms, two to three minutes, then turn it once. Baste with butter or brush with oil, because the flesh is lean and loses moisture fast. Take it off while the very centre is still faintly translucent, about 52 to 54°C (126 to 129°F), and rest it for three or four minutes; the heat travels inward and the centre turns opaque and just moist.

That is below the Food Code's 63°C (145°F) for 15 seconds, the figure for fish cooked through: a steak served under it goes out under the consumer advisory, and the house's own temperature is learned at lineup.

Grenobloise, say gruh-no-BLWAZ, of Grenoble, is the meunière's cousin. Meunière is fish dusted in flour, cooked in butter and finished with brown butter, lemon and parsley; Grenobloise keeps all of that and adds capers for salt, croutons for crunch and often lemon segments. The croutons go on last so they stay crisp. It names a treatment, not a fish: sole is the classic, and any firm fillet or steak takes it.

Dry, fibrous and chalky: overcooked, the usual fault; pull it earlier, baste it and rest it. No crust: a wet surface or a pan not hot enough. A strong, metallic taste: the bloodline left in. Mushy: a steak cut too thin, or a fish past its best. A bitter garnish: brown butter taken past hazelnut; stop it with lemon the moment it smells nutty.

Swordfish is a large predator at the top of its food chain, so it carries more mercury than small fish, and the FDA's advice on eating fish lists it among the choices to avoid for women who are pregnant or may become pregnant, those breastfeeding and young children. On the floor it is never answered from memory: the kitchen and the service note hold the answer, so go and ask.

The North Atlantic swordfish is a recovery story. By the late 1990s the stock had fallen to roughly 58 to 65 per cent of the level that gives the maximum sustainable yield, and in January 1998 SeaWeb and the Natural Resources Defense Council launched Give Swordfish a Break, a pledge that drew hundreds of chefs and restaurants to take it off their menus. An international rebuilding plan followed in 1999, and NOAA now describes the stock as rebuilt and calls US-caught swordfish a sustainable choice. Where tonight's fish was caught is not printed; the kitchen says.

At Brennan's the fall Swordfish Grenobloise sets a firm swordfish fillet on a leek fondue, say fon-DOO, leeks melted slowly in butter until soft and sweet, with brown butter, lemon, fried capers, parsley and croutons cut from Leidenheimer bread. It prints no catch area, portion or cooking method, so claim none, learn the kitchen's cut and method at lineup, and never repeat the story that the garnish was invented to hide bad fish.

Say firm, meaty and mildly sweet, never strong, and offer it to the guest who wants fish with some substance. Describe the garnish as nutty brown butter, lemon, crisp salty capers and crunch. A guest who asks for it well done should hear that it will be drier; the kitchen can say how far it will take it.

ratios.label: Steak thickness
ratios.value: About 3 cm (1 1/4 inches), never under 2.5 cm (1 inch)

ratios.label: Sear
ratios.value: Two to three minutes a side in a smoking-hot pan or on a hot grill, turned once

ratios.label: Rest
ratios.value: Three to four minutes, as for a steak

temps.label: Pull the steak from the heat at about
The Food Code's figure for fish cooked through, held 15 seconds

faults.cause: Overcooked: the centre went opaque in the pan and kept cooking in the rest.
faults.fix: Pull it while the centre is still faintly translucent, baste with fat and rest it three or four minutes.

faults.cause: A wet surface, or a pan that was not hot enough.
faults.fix: Pat the steak dry, salt and oil it, and wait for the pan to smoke before it goes in.

faults.cause: The dark bloodline was left in the steak.
faults.fix: Trim the bloodline out before cooking, and take the tough skin off with it.

faults.fault: Bitter brown butter on the garnish
faults.cause: The butter was taken past hazelnut to burnt.
faults.fix: Stop it with lemon the moment it smells nutty; a burnt batch is thrown out and started again.

It flakes apart at a touch

entries.title: Tuna
entries.summary: The tunas a kitchen names by colour, fat and price: yellowfin, bigeye, albacore and bluefin. Firm and meaty, deep red to pale pink, and the fish most often served raw, so its handling and its advisory matter as much as any cooking.
entries.guest: Our tuna is served raw, as a crudo, under a carrot and ginger aguachile, a sweet, warm, chilli-bright sauce, with burnt orange, pickled pearl onions and a flake of salt.

paras: Tuna is a family of large, fast ocean fish with firm, meaty flesh that runs from deep red to pale pink. A kitchen names four. Yellowfin, ahi, say AH-hee, in Hawaii, is the workhorse: lean, pink to red and mild, the usual tuna for a seared steak or crudo. Bigeye, also sold as ahi, is deeper in colour and fattier, the better raw fish of the two. Albacore is the palest and softest, the white tuna of the tin. Bluefin is the deepest red and the fattiest, and the dearest. Skipjack, small and strong, is the light tuna of the tin.

Sashimi-grade and sushi-grade are market words, not a legal grade: no United States agency defines them. They mean a supplier's promise that the fish was handled for raw service and say nothing about parasites or origin, so the house's own handling does the real work. In Japanese grading of the loin akami, say ah-KAH-mee, is the lean red meat of the back; chūtoro, say CHOO-toh-roh, is the medium-fatty meat towards the belly; and ōtoro, say OH-toh-roh, the fattiest belly, pale, marbled and dear. Look for a glossy, translucent cut face and a clean smell; brown edges, a rainbow sheen or gaps between the muscle layers mean age.

Bluefin stocks have been heavily fished and are managed under international quotas; guides such as Seafood Watch rate yellowfin and bigeye fishery by fishery, and rate pole-and-line and troll-caught fish better than longline and purse seine. A Marine Stewardship Council label names a certified fishery. Which fishery, gear and label stand behind tonight's tuna is the kitchen's to confirm; a server claims none.

Mercury rises with a fish's size: the FDA's advice on eating fish lists bigeye tuna among the choices to avoid in pregnancy, when breastfeeding and for young children, with yellowfin and albacore among its good choices; bluefin is not on its chart. The species is not printed, so that question goes to the kitchen and the service note.

Raw service lives at the cold edge. Tuna for crudo is held at or below 5°C (41°F), portioned on a chilled board with a chilled blade, sliced across the grain in one pull and dressed at the last moment; a slice that waits warms, weeps and dulls. The Food Code's answer to parasites in fish served raw is freezing, hard and long; the figures are below. The same code exempts the named tunas, yellowfin, bigeye, albacore and the bluefins among them, so whether tonight's fish was frozen, and which species and cut it is, are lineup questions, never guesses.

Three raw dishes differ in what the liquid does. Crudo, say KROO-doh, the Italian word for raw, is fish sliced and dressed at the last moment with oil, acid and salt; the acid only seasons it. Ceviche, say seh-VEE-chay, steeps fish in citrus until the acid turns the surface opaque and firm; nothing is heated, so the fish is cured, not cooked, and the advisory still stands. Aguachile, say ah-gwah-CHEE-leh, chilli water, is the raw shrimp dish of Sinaloa on Mexico's Pacific coast: lime blended with fresh chilli, poured over and eaten at once. Never say the citrus cooks the fish.

Dull, brown, soft fish: age or warmth, not for raw service. Mushy slices: cut with the grain or with a dragging blade. A weeping, grey crudo: dressed or salted too early. Chewy pieces: sinew from the tail of the loin; cut from the thicker end.

At Brennan's the Fall 2026 tasting carries a Tuna Crudo: raw tuna under a carrot and ginger aguachile, with salsa seca, say SAL-sah SEH-kah, a dry salsa of toasted chillies and seeds, burnt orange segments, pickled pearl onions, coriander and Maldon salt. The pack prints tuna and no more: not the species, the cut, the catch or whether the kitchen cures it briefly, so promise none of that. What is in the salsa seca goes to the service note and the kitchen, and so do the sheet's dietary marks, which leave fish off this plate: raise that at lineup and keep fish in any guest conversation.

Say raw first, then the consumer advisory, before the order goes in. Then the words: crudo, raw; aguachile, chilli water, ours with carrot for sweetness and ginger for warmth; salsa seca for crunch. Confirm the heat with the kitchen before you call it mild. A guest who asks what kind of tuna, where it came from or whether it was frozen gets the kitchen's answer.

ratios.label: Slice for crudo

ratios.label: A crudo dressing

ratios.label: Freezing for parasites, where the kitchen freezes

temps.label: Cold holding for raw fish, at or below
Food Code parasite freeze, seven days at or below

faults.cause: Age, or time spent above the cold edge.
faults.fix: It is not for raw service; tell the chef. Hold tuna at or below 5°C (41°F) and use it fast.

faults.cause: Cut with the grain, or with a dragging blade.
faults.fix: A chilled, sharp blade, across the grain, one pull for each slice.

cards.front: What does sashimi-grade mean?
cards.back: A market word, not a legal grade: a supplier's promise that the fish was handled for raw service. It says nothing about parasites or origin, so the house's own handling does the real work.

cards.front: What are akami, chūtoro and ōtoro?
cards.back: Cuts of the loin by fat: akami the lean red back, chūtoro the medium-fatty meat towards the belly, ōtoro the fattiest belly, pale, marbled and dear.

cards.front: How is tuna for crudo handled?
cards.back: Held at or below 5°C (41°F), portioned on a chilled board with a chilled blade, sliced across the grain in one pull and dressed at the last moment.

cards.front: What is the Food Code's answer to parasites in raw fish, and where do the tunas stand?
cards.back: Freezing, hard and long, before service; the code exempts the named tunas, so whether tonight's fish was frozen is a lineup question, never a guess.

cards.front: How do crudo, ceviche and aguachile differ?
cards.back: Crudo is dressed at the last moment with oil, acid and salt; ceviche steeps in citrus until the surface turns opaque; aguachile pours chilli and lime water over and is eaten at once. None is cooked.

cards.front: Does the aguachile cook the tuna?
cards.back: No. Acid firms and whitens the surface of a fish but adds no heat; the tuna is raw, the advisory stands, and the citrus is never called cooking.

cards.front: What does a server say first about the Tuna Crudo?
cards.back: That it is raw, then the consumer advisory, before the order goes in; then the words crudo and aguachile, and the sauce.

cards.front: A guest asks whether the tuna is sustainably caught. What do you say?
cards.back: That the fishery, the gear and any label are the kitchen's to confirm, and go and ask; guides such as Seafood Watch rate pole-and-line and troll-caught fish better than longline or purse seine, but claim nothing for tonight's fish.

cards.front: A pregnant guest asks whether the Tuna Crudo is all right for her. What do you do?
cards.back: Never answer from the floor. Mercury rises with a fish's size, and the FDA lists bigeye tuna among the choices to avoid in pregnancy; the species is not printed, so the kitchen and the service note hold the answer.

cards.front: Why does a crudo weep and turn grey?
cards.back: Dressed or salted too early: salt and acid pull water from the fish. Slice and dress at the pass, salt last, and send it at once.

cards.front: What is on the Brennan's Tuna Crudo?
cards.back: Raw tuna under a carrot and ginger aguachile, with salsa seca, burnt orange segments, pickled pearl onions, coriander and Maldon salt. Species, cut, catch and any curing are not printed.

questions.q: Which tuna is the deepest red, the fattiest and the dearest?
questions.answer: Bluefin
questions.why: Bluefin is the sushi counter's prize and the dearest fish on any list; albacore is the palest, yellowfin the lean workhorse, and skipjack the light tuna of the tin.

questions.q: What does sashimi-grade on a tuna invoice tell you?
questions.answer: A supplier's promise, not a legal grade
distractors: The fish was frozen for parasites
questions.why: No US agency defines sashimi-grade; it is a market word for fish handled for raw service, and says nothing about parasites or origin.

questions.q: Which cut of the tuna loin is the fattiest?
questions.answer: Ōtoro, the belly
questions.why: Ōtoro is the fattiest belly, pale, marbled and dear; akami is the lean red back and chūtoro the medium-fatty meat between them.

questions.q: How should tuna for crudo be sliced?
questions.answer: Across the grain, one pull each, on a chilled board
distractors: With the grain, in a sawing motion
At room temperature, so it softens
After it has been dressed and salted
questions.why: A chilled blade across the grain in one pull keeps the slice clean; sawing or cutting with the grain tears it, and warmth or early dressing makes it weep.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the tuna was frozen before it was served raw. What is the answer?
questions.answer: Ask the kitchen; the code exempts the tunas
distractors: Yes, all raw fish must be frozen
questions.why: The Food Code's parasite rule is freezing, but it exempts the named tunas, so whether this house freezes its tuna is the kitchen's answer, never a guess from the floor.

questions.q: A guest who is pregnant asks whether the Tuna Crudo is all right for her. What does a server do?
questions.answer: Go to the kitchen and the service note
distractors: Say yes, since yellowfin is a good choice
Say no, all tuna is on the avoid list
questions.why: Mercury rises with size and the FDA lists bigeye among the choices to avoid, but the species is not printed, so the answer is never given from the floor.

questions.q: What separates a crudo from a ceviche?
questions.answer: Crudo is dressed at the last moment; ceviche steeps
distractors: Crudo is cooked; ceviche is raw
Crudo uses lime; ceviche uses oil
Ceviche is always made with tuna
questions.why: A crudo is sliced and dressed with oil, acid and salt as it goes out; a ceviche steeps in citrus until the surface turns opaque. Neither is cooked.

questions.q: What is the first thing a server says about the Tuna Crudo?
questions.answer: That it is raw, with the consumer advisory
distractors: That it is the chef's favourite
questions.why: Crudo means raw, and the advisory goes before the order; the aguachile dresses the fish and never cooks it, so the citrus is never called cooking.

questions.q: Which of these does the Brennan's pack print about the Tuna Crudo?
questions.answer: A carrot and ginger aguachile
distractors: That the tuna is cured first
questions.why: The pack names the aguachile, salsa seca, burnt orange, pickled pearl onions, coriander and Maldon salt; the species, the cut, the catch and any curing are not printed.
